title: Testicular torsion and the acute scrotum
subtitle: Torsion until the theatre says otherwise

sources.org: European Association of Urology (EAU) and European Society for Paediatric Urology (ESPU)
sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology: acute scrotum in children

sources.org: The Journal of Urology (Barbosa JA et al.)
sources.title: Development and initial validation of a scoring system to diagnose testicular torsion in children (TWIST)
EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections: epididymitis and orchitis

red_flags.text: Sudden severe testicular pain, especially waking from sleep, in a child, adolescent or young man.
Nausea and vomiting with scrotal pain. This is far more typical of torsion than of epididymitis.
A high-riding testis with a horizontal lie, or an absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side.
Abdominal pain in a boy: always examine the scrotum. Torsion often presents as lower abdominal pain, and adolescents may not volunteer the site.
An empty hemiscrotum with groin pain: torsion of an undescended testis.
Previous episodes of short-lived severe testicular pain that settled: intermittent torsion, which needs fixing electively before the episode that does not settle.

do_now.text: Treat suspected torsion as a surgical emergency. Inform the operating surgeon and theatre immediately; testicular salvage falls steeply with every hour of ischaemia.
Do not delay exploration for an ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high. Doppler is operator-dependent and a normal-looking flow does not exclude partial or intermittent torsion.
Keep the patient nil by mouth, give analgesia, and take consent for exploration, bilateral fixation and possible orchidectomy before the patient reaches theatre.
Manual detorsion may be attempted as a temporising manoeuvre if theatre is delayed, but it does not replace exploration and fixation.

assess.text: Time of onset to the nearest hour. It is the most important prognostic fact and must be documented.

A structured clinical score helps the decision: testicular swelling, hard testis, absent cremasteric reflex, nausea or vomiting, and a high-riding testis. A high score supports going straight to theatre; a low score makes torsion unlikely but does not exclude it.

Look for alternatives without letting them become the comfortable explanation: torsion of an appendix testis (the blue dot sign, pain localised to the upper pole), epididymo-orchitis (urinary symptoms, gradual onset, sexual history), trauma, hernia and tumour.
In a neonate, a firm painless swollen testis is usually prenatal extravaginal torsion. Discuss with paediatric urology the same day.

investigate.text: Urine dipstick and culture. A positive dipstick does not exclude torsion.
Doppler ultrasound only when suspicion is low or intermediate and it will not delay theatre. It is useful to support an alternative diagnosis, not to rule torsion out.
Sexually transmitted infection testing in sexually active patients with suspected epididymitis.

resuscitate.text: Adequate analgesia before examination and before any attempt at manual detorsion; a distressed adolescent cannot be examined well.

definitive.text: Scrotal exploration: untwist, assess viability after warming, fix the testis if it is viable, and fix the contralateral testis at the same operation.
Remove a clearly necrotic testis. Leaving a dead testis risks infection, abscess and prolonged pain.
Torsion of an appendix testis confirmed clinically or on scan can be managed conservatively with analgesia; explore if there is any doubt.
Epididymo-orchitis is treated with antibiotics chosen by age and sexual risk per guideline, but only once torsion has been excluded with confidence.

escalate.text: Senior urologist or paediatric surgeon on call now, not at the morning handover.
If the receiving hospital cannot operate within a short time, the nearest surgeon who can explore the scrotum should do it. Transfer for subspecialty care costs testes.
Neonatal torsion and torsion of an undescended testis: paediatric urology or paediatric surgery.

notes: The clinical score cuts both ways. A boy with a high score goes to theatre without a scan; a boy with a low score still gets explored if the examining surgeon is worried.
A negative exploration is a good outcome. A missed torsion is a lost testis and a medicolegal case, and the commonest reason is a reassuring ultrasound.
Manual detorsion is usually outwards, like opening a book, but torsion can occur in either direction. Relief of pain is the guide; if pain worsens, try the other way.
